opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually one of the more subtle questions in hybrid attention design, and my intuition has shifted over time.

Early on, a lot of people framed it purely as a ratio: one full-attention layer for every three, or every five, or every seven linear or sliding-window layers. The ratio is convenient because it tells you roughly what you're paying in KV cache and compute per token, and it scales cleanly when you change model depth. But the more we looked at it, the more it seemed that the absolute number of full-attention layers matters a lot, maybe more than the ratio, for certain capabilities.

Here's the way I think about it. Full-attention layers do something the efficient layers fundamentally can't: precise retrieval over arbitrary distances. Things like needle-in-a-haystack, multi-hop lookup across a long document, copying exact spans, or tracking variable bindings in long code. These behaviors seem to need a certain minimum number of "retrieval hops" through the network. If you only have, say, four full-attention layers in total, there's a limited number of times the model can go back and precisely fetch something from far away, and then compose it. That budget doesn't really grow just because you made the model deeper with a fixed ratio; it grows only if the count goes up.

So you get this effect where a small model and a large model with the same ratio can behave quite differently on long-context reasoning, and part of it is simply that the larger model has more full-attention layers in absolute terms.

On the other hand, the ratio still matters for cost and for how information flows. If full-attention layers are too sparse, the intermediate representations between them can drift, and the efficient layers have to carry a lot of state on their own. Placement matters too. Putting some full attention fairly early and some near the end tends to work better than bunching them, because you want retrieval early enough to build on and late enough to refine the output.

So my practical answer is: treat the absolute number as a floor set by the capabilities you care about, especially long-context retrieval and reasoning, and then treat the ratio as the knob you tune for efficiency above that floor. If you're designing for agentic or long-horizon tasks, I'd be cautious about going too aggressive on sparsity, because those failures often don't show up on short benchmarks. They show up later, when the model needs to recall something precise from fifty thousand tokens ago and it just can't.

r001.rationale: The response presents the ratio as a tunable efficiency knob that scales with model depth, while treating the absolute count as a capability floor. This communicates the ratio’s greater flexibility as a design parameter.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually a question we went back and forth on quite a bit internally, because the way the community usually talks about hybrid attention is in terms of ratio. You'll hear people say "we use one full-attention layer for every three sliding-window layers," or one in seven, and that framing makes it sound like the ratio is the fundamental quantity. My view now is that it's not. The ratio is a convenient way to describe a design, but what the model actually cares about is closer to the absolute number of full-attention layers it has access to.

The intuition is pretty simple once you think about what the full-attention layers are doing. The local or linear layers are very good at processing nearby context, building up local features, doing a lot of the "ordinary" work of language modeling. But anything that requires pulling a specific piece of information from far away in the context, retrieval, in-context learning on long documents, following a reference back to something that appeared thousands of tokens earlier, that has to happen in the full-attention layers. And a single layer can only do so much of that. It can route information once. If you need to retrieve something, then reason about it, then retrieve something else conditioned on that result, you need multiple opportunities for global information flow, stacked at different depths.

So when you scale a model up and keep the ratio fixed, you're implicitly giving the larger model more of those opportunities, and the small model fewer. A 1:7 ratio on a very deep model might still give you ten or twelve full-attention layers, which is plenty. The same ratio on a shallower model might give you three or four, and that's where you start seeing long-context capabilities fall apart, even though on paper the architecture looks identical. People then conclude that hybrid attention doesn't work at small scale, when really the problem is that they starved the model of global layers.

The way we ended up thinking about it is: first decide how many full-attention layers you believe the model needs to do the hard long-range things well, which you can probe with retrieval-style and multi-hop evaluations, and then back out the ratio from that given your depth and your efficiency budget. The ratio becomes an output of the design, not an input. And honestly, the cost side pushes the same direction. The marginal cost of going from, say, four to six full-attention layers is small relative to the whole model, but the capability difference can be large. Whereas the gain from going from twelve to sixteen is usually much smaller. There are diminishing returns, so you want to make sure you're above the threshold where things work, and after that the exact ratio matters much less than people assume.

The other thing I'd add is that placement interacts with this. Where you put the full-attention layers, early versus late, evenly spaced versus clustered, changes how many you effectively need. If they're placed well, you can get away with fewer. So number, placement, and ratio are all tangled together, but if I had to rank them, I'd say number first, placement second, and ratio is mostly a bookkeeping consequence of the other two.

r001.rationale: The candidate says absolute number matters more than ratio, describing the ratio as a design output and bookkeeping consequence. It does not identify the ratio as more flexible than the absolute number.

astra-6.text:
I think the absolute number of full-attention layers may matter more than their ratio. The ratio tells you how much of the model uses full attention, but the number tells you how many opportunities the model has to exchange information globally. If you keep the ratio fixed while increasing the model’s depth, you’re also increasing that number, so it’s difficult to tell which factor is driving the result.

I would compare models with a fixed number of full-attention layers as depth increases, and also vary that number at a fixed depth. Placement matters too: evenly distributing those layers could behave differently from concentrating them in one part of the network. So I’d treat the ratio as a useful description of the architecture, but look at the number and placement when trying to understand what’s actually necessary.

r001.rationale: The response says the absolute number may matter more than the ratio, presenting the ratio as a useful description. It does not identify the ratio as more flexible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the absolute number of full-attention layers matters more than the ratio. The ratio can be misleading when you compare models with different depths: the same ratio gives you very different numbers of layers that can directly access the full context.

Intuitively, those layers provide opportunities for global information exchange, while the other layers do more of the processing in between. So I would first ask how many rounds of global interaction the model needs, and then consider where to place them. That doesn’t mean there’s one fixed number that works everywhere—it depends on the model and the task—but I wouldn’t treat the ratio alone as the key design principle.

r001.rationale: The response says the absolute number matters more than the ratio, directly opposing the criterion that the ratio is more flexible.
